Abbreviations for internet/networking (HTTP, URL, ISP...) are collected in the internet-email and networking topics.

tricks.title: ROM family ladder
tricks.body: P -> EP -> EEPROM: each generation gets *easier* to erase - PROM (once, at manufacture/programming), EPROM (erase with **UV light**), EEPROM (erase **electrically**, in circuit). "UV for EPROM, Electricity for EEPROM."

example.q: EPROM is erased using?
example.solution: Ultraviolet light.

tricks.title: OCR-OMR-MICR trio
tricks.body: OCR reads **Characters** (printed text -> editable text), OMR reads **Marks** (exam bubbles), MICR reads **Ink** on **cheques** (banks). Characters, Marks, Ink = CRM.

example.q: Bank cheque reading uses?
example.solution: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition).

mistakes: Expanding UPS as 'Uninterrupted' - the accepted form is **Uninterruptible** Power Supply.
Reading POST as 'Power On System Test' - it is **Power-On Self-Test**.
Confusing DPI (dots per inch, printers) with PPI (pixels per inch, screens).
subtopics.notes:
### Why this subtopic is pure marks
Every exam asks 1–3 direct full-form questions. There is no logic to apply — only a table to know. Learn them in families so one wrong expansion cannot slip past you.

### CPU and system family
| Short | Full form |
|---|---|
| CPU / ALU / CU | Central Processing Unit / Arithmetic Logic Unit / Control Unit |
| BIOS | Basic Input Output System |
| POST | **Power-On Self-Test** (not 'Power On System Test') |
| UPS | **Uninterruptible** Power Supply (not 'Uninterrupted') |
| USB | Universal Serial Bus |
| GUI | Graphical User Interface |

### Memory family
| Short | Full form |
|---|---|
| RAM / ROM | Random Access Memory / Read Only Memory |
| PROM / EPROM / EEPROM | (Erasable) (Electrically Erasable) Programmable Read Only Memory |
| SRAM / DRAM | Static / Dynamic RAM |
| Cache | Fast memory between CPU and RAM (not an abbreviation) |

### Device and media family
| Short | Full form |
|---|---|
| VDU | Visual Display Unit (the monitor) |
| LCD / LED | Liquid Crystal Display / Light Emitting Diode |
| CRT | Cathode Ray Tube (the old heavy monitors) |
| HDD / SSD | Hard Disk Drive / Solid State Drive |
| CD / DVD | Compact Disc / Digital Versatile Disc |
| OCR / OMR / MICR | Optical Character Recognition / Optical Mark Recognition / Magnetic Ink Character Recognition |
| DPI / PPI | Dots Per Inch (printers) / Pixels Per Inch (screens) |

### How wrong options are built
Exams do not ask tricky full forms — they ask **plausible wrong ones**:
- UPS → 'Uninterrupted' (correct: **Uninterruptible**).
- POST → 'Power On System Test' (correct: **Power-On Self-Test**).
- VDU → 'Video Display Unit' (correct: **Visual** Display Unit).
- PPI for printers (PPI is for screens; printers use **DPI**).
Read every word of every option — one wrong adjective decides the answer.

### Two memory hooks that settle half the family questions
- **Reader trio:** OCR reads **C**haracters (a scanned page becomes editable text), OMR reads **M**arks (bubble answer sheets), MICR reads magnetic **I**nk (the code line at the bottom of bank cheques). C–M–I: Characters, Marks, Ink.
- **ROM ladder:** PROM can be programmed **once**; **EP**ROM is erased with **U**ltraviolet light; **EEP**ROM is erased **electrically**, right in the circuit. Each step makes erasing easier — that single idea answers every PROM/EPROM/EEPROM question.

### A five-second checking habit
1. Expand the letters yourself **before** looking at the options.
2. Match word by word — first noun, then every adjective.
3. If two options differ by one word (Uninterrupted/Uninterruptible), trust the table, not the ear.

### Quick revision
- CPU/ALU/CU, BIOS, GUI, USB — know them cold.
- UPS = Uninterruptible; POST = Power-On Self-Test; VDU = Visual Display Unit.
- ROM ladder: PROM (program once) → EPROM (erase with UV light) → EEPROM (erase electrically).
- OCR = Characters, OMR = Marks, MICR = magnetic **Ink on cheques**.
- DPI = printers (dots); PPI = screens (pixels).

patterns.name: Direct full-form recall
patterns.howToSpot: 'What is the full form of BIOS / ALU / GUI / USB?' — a plain expansion question with four expansions.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the family table the abbreviation belongs to (CPU family, memory family, device family).
2. Expand letter by letter and compare word by word; do not recognise the option 'as a whole'.
3. BIOS = Basic Input Output System; GUI = Graphical User Interface; USB = Universal Serial Bus.

example.q: The full form of **GUI** is —
example.solution: **Graphical User Interface** — the windows-icons-menus-pointer style of working, as against typing commands.

patterns.name: Plausible-wrong expansion traps
patterns.howToSpot: All four options look almost identical — the wrong ones change one adjective (Uninterrupted/Uninterruptible, Power On System Test/Power-On Self-Test, Video/Visual).
patterns.logic:
1. Read every word of each option; the trap is one swapped word.
2. Fixed traps: UPS = **Uninterruptible** Power Supply; POST = **Power-On Self-Test**; VDU = **Visual** Display Unit.
3. If two options look nearly right, the longer-worded standard form is usually correct (Uninterruptible, Self-Test).

example.q: The accepted full form of **UPS** is —
example.solution: **Uninterruptible Power Supply** — a battery backup that switches in instantly when mains power fails. 'Uninterrupted' is the planted trap.

patterns.name: Abbreviation ↔ device/domain matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'DPI measures…', 'MICR is used in…', 'VDU refers to…' — the abbreviation is given with its use or device asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Reader trio: OCR = characters (scanned text), OMR = marks (exam bubbles), MICR = magnetic ink (bank cheques).
2. Resolution pair: DPI = dots per inch → printers; PPI = pixels per inch → screens.
3. VDU = the monitor; BIOS = firmware chip that starts the machine.

example.q: **MICR** technology is used mainly in —
example.solution: **Cheque processing in banks** — MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) reads the characters printed at the bottom of a cheque in special magnetic ink.

patterns.name: Odd one out / mismatched pair among abbreviations
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is not a memory term?', 'which pair is wrongly matched?' — one option breaks the family.
patterns.logic:
1. Test each option's full form against the family table.
2. Memory family: RAM, ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, SRAM, DRAM, Cache. Anything else (RTOS, HTTP, GUI) breaks the family.
3. For mismatched pairs, expand both halves and compare word by word.

example.q: Which of the following is **NOT** related to memory?
example.solution: **RTOS** — Real-Time Operating System, an OS type. RAM, ROM, PROM and DRAM are all memory terms.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem names a technology (vacuum tube, transistor, IC, microprocessor) or a machine (ENIAC, IBM 360) and asks its generation, or the reverse. Statement variants ask which feature belongs to which generation.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the ladder vacuum tube (1st) → transistor (2nd) → IC (3rd) → microprocessor (4th) → AI (5th) and match the technology first, the years second — year ranges differ between books but the technology order never does.

example.q: Third-generation computers were built around:
example.solution: Integrated Circuits (ICs) — whole circuits printed on one silicon chip; they brought keyboards, monitors and operating systems.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'What is the full form of BIOS / ALU / MICR / UPS?' or a wrongly-matched pair where one expansion has one wrong word.
pyqPatterns.approach: Expand letter by letter from the family table (CPU family, memory family, device family). The classic traps: UPS = Uninterruptible (not Uninterrupted), POST = Power-On Self-Test (not Power On System Test), VDU = Visual (not Video).

example.q: The full form of POST is:
example.solution: Power-On Self-Test — the start-up diagnostic that checks hardware before the OS loads.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'First commercial computer', 'first electronic digital computer', 'first microprocessor', 'first stored-program computer' — a superlative with machine names as options.
pyqPatterns.approach: Keep the firsts chain pinned: ABC 1942 (first electronic digital) → ENIAC 1946 (first general-purpose electronic) → EDSAC 1949 (first stored-program) → UNIVAC-I 1951 (first commercial) → Intel 4004 1971 (first microprocessor). Read the exact adjective in the stem.

example.q: Which machine is regarded as the first commercially available computer?
example.solution: UNIVAC-I (1951) — ENIAC was earlier but experimental; UNIVAC-I was the first sold to businesses.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which unit performs arithmetic or comparison?', 'which register holds the next address?', 'the correct order of fetch/decode/execute/store'.
pyqPatterns.approach: CPU = ALU (all maths and logic) + CU (direction only, no calculation) + registers (fastest storage). The cycle is always Fetch → Decode → Execute → Store; reversed Decode/Fetch or Execute/Store pairs are the planted traps.

example.q: In the machine cycle, the step that interprets what the instruction means is:
example.solution: Decode — done by the Control Unit, between Fetch (bring it) and Execute (do it).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which is not a programming language?', 'which is not a translator?', 'which one is a markup language?' — three options from one family, one from another.
pyqPatterns.approach: Classify each option first: HTML = markup (not programming); assembler = assembly-language translator; compiler/interpreter = high-level translators. The odd option is usually a famous name placed in the wrong family.

example.q: Which of the following is not a translator?
example.solution: HTML — it is a markup language. Assembler, compiler and interpreter are all translators.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A workplace or workload is described — bank records, railway reservation (mainframe), weather forecasting (supercomputer), a single user's laptop (micro), a hybrid petrol-pump unit — and the class is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use the two ladders: size (Super → Mainframe → Mini → Micro) and principle (analog measures continuous, digital counts 0/1, hybrid does both). Bulk transactions for thousands of users = mainframe; one enormous calculation = supercomputer.

example.q: A petrol-pump machine that measures fuel flow continuously and prints the price digitally is a:
example.solution: Hybrid computer — analog measurement combined with digital computation.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who invented the mouse / WWW / punched cards?', 'the first programmer was', 'SQL belongs to which language generation?' — name-contribution or language-level pairs.
pyqPatterns.approach: Hold the pioneer table (Babbage, Ada, Turing, von Neumann, Hopper, Berners-Lee, Engelbart, Hollerith) and the GL ladder (1GL machine → 2GL assembly → 3GL high-level → 4GL SQL → 5GL AI). Watch the classic swaps: Ada vs Hopper, WWW vs Internet, HTML vs programming language.

example.q: The first-generation (1GL) language that needs no translator is:
example.solution: Machine language — pure 0s and 1s executed directly by the CPU; assembly (2GL) needs an assembler.

solvedExamples.q:
Arrange the computer generations in order of their defining technology:
A. Integrated Circuits  B. Vacuum Tubes  C. Microprocessor  D. Transistors
solvedExamples.solution: Generation order: 1st vacuum tubes (B) -> 2nd transistors (D) -> 3rd ICs (A) -> 4th microprocessor (C). So the sequence B-D-A-C is correct.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Ladder mnemonic "Very Tiny ICs Made AI" - just map the four options onto the ladder; no dates needed.

solvedExamples.q:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. ENIAC was the first general-purpose electronic digital computer.
2. UNIVAC-I was the first computer to use vacuum tubes.
solvedExamples.solution: Statement 1 is correct - ENIAC (1946) was the first general-purpose electronic digital computer. Statement 2 is wrong: UNIVAC-I (1951) was the first *commercial* computer, and vacuum tubes were the 1st-generation technology used already by ENIAC.
solvedExamples.shortcut: If a statement pairs UNIVAC with 'first', check the exact phrase: 'first commercial' is right, almost anything else ('first computer', 'first vacuum-tube computer') is the trap.

solvedExamples.q: Which CPU unit coordinates and controls all parts of the computer but does not itself perform calculations?
solvedExamples.solution: The Control Unit directs the flow of data and instructions and coordinates all units; actual arithmetic/logic is done by the ALU. Registers are tiny storage locations, and memory only holds data.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 'Coordinates/controls/directs' -> CU; 'calculates/compares' -> ALU. The verbs in the question are the answer.

solvedExamples.q: In a language translated line by line with execution stopping at the first erroneous line, the translator is a:
solvedExamples.solution: An interpreter converts and executes high-level code one line at a time and halts at the first error. A compiler translates the entire program before execution (reporting all errors together), an assembler handles assembly language, and a linker joins compiled modules.
solvedExamples.shortcut: "Line by line" in the question points straight to interpreter; "whole program at once" would mean compiler.

practice.q: Transistors were used as the basic technology of which generation of computers?
practice.solution: The 2nd generation (1956-63) replaced vacuum tubes with transistors, making computers smaller, faster and more reliable. 1st = vacuum tubes, 3rd = ICs, 4th = microprocessors.
practice.shortcut: Generation ladder: Vacuum -> Transistor -> IC -> Microprocessor -> AI. Transistor is the 2nd rung.

practice.q: ENIAC, completed in 1946, stands for:
options: Electronic Number Integrating and Computing Engine
Electronic Numerical Index Analyser and Computer
practice.solution: ENIAC = Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer, built by Eckert and Mauchly at the University of Pennsylvania.
practice.shortcut: Trap options all start with 'Electronic/Electrical'; remember the key words 'Numerical Integrator And Computer'.

practice.q: Which of the following is regarded as the first commercially available computer?
practice.solution: UNIVAC-I (1951) was the first computer produced and sold commercially. ENIAC was a one-off military project; EDVAC was a stored-program research machine; IBM 360 is a 3rd-generation family (1964).
practice.shortcut: UNIVAC = the first computer you could BUY; ENIAC = the first one ever BUILT electronically.

practice.q: The Intel 4004, released in 1971, is historically important because it was the first:
practice.solution: Intel 4004 (1971) was the world's first commercially available microprocessor - an entire CPU on one chip - and it launched the 4th generation of computers.
practice.shortcut: 4004 = 4th generation's flag-bearer: 'the 4004 started Gen 4'.

practice.q: Which of the following areas characterises fifth-generation computers?
practice.solution: The 5th generation targets AI, natural-language processing, parallel and quantum-style computing. Punched cards belong to the pre-1st/1st era, assembly is a 2nd-generation language habit, and vacuum tubes are 1st generation.
practice.shortcut: Anything with 'intelligence, learning, robotics, parallel' = 5th generation.

practice.q: PARAM 8000, India's first indigenous supercomputer (1991), was developed by:
practice.solution: PARAM 8000 was built in 1991 by C-DAC (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing), Pune, under Dr Vijay Bhatkar, after the USA denied Cray supercomputer imports.
practice.shortcut: PARAM always pairs with C-DAC; the denial story (' PARAM = Perform Anvaya Reusable Module') is extra trivia - the developer is what SSC asks.

practice.q: Banks handling lakhs of cheque and transaction records centrally typically deploy:
practice.solution: Mainframes (e.g. IBM zSeries) are built for very high-volume, reliable, simultaneous transaction processing - exactly banking, railways and census workloads.
practice.shortcut: Bulk transactions -> mainframe; raw scientific speed -> supercomputer; one appliance control -> embedded/microcontroller.

practice.q: A device that measures continuous physical quantities like temperature or pressure and outputs a voltage-based result is classified as:
practice.solution: Analog computers work on continuous signals (voltage, speed, temperature) rather than discrete 0/1 digits. Hybrid machines combine analog measurement with digital processing; quantum computers use qubits.
practice.shortcut: 'Continuous quantities' is the keyword for analog; 'counts with digits 0/1' means digital.

practice.q: Which part of the CPU performs subtraction and comparison operations?
practice.solution: Arithmetic (add, subtract) and logical (compare, AND/OR) operations are executed in the ALU. The program counter is a register holding the next instruction's address; the CU only coordinates.
practice.shortcut: Any verb like add/subtract/compare/AND-OR -> ALU, no matter how the question dresses it up.

practice.q: The correct sequence of steps in a single machine cycle is:
practice.solution: The CPU first Fetches the instruction from memory, Decodes it in the control unit, Executes it in the ALU, and Stores the result.
practice.shortcut: Fat Dogs Eat Snacks: Fetch -> Decode -> Execute -> Store. Any option starting with Decode/Execute is out.

practice.q: Assembly language mnemonics such as ADD and MOV are converted into machine code by a(n):
practice.solution: An assembler translates assembly (2GL) mnemonics into machine language. Compilers/interpreters work on high-level (3GL) languages; preprocessors transform source text before compilation.
practice.shortcut: Assembly -> Assembler (same first letters); high-level -> compiler/interpreter.

practice.q: Which of the following is a markup language rather than a programming language?
practice.solution: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) only structures and presents content using tags; it has no logic/control-flow constructs of its own, so it is a markup language. Python, C++ and Java are programming languages.
practice.shortcut: Markup = tags for layout (HTML, XML, Markdown). If the option 'structures web pages', it is not a programming language.

practice.q: Who is known as the first computer programmer for her notes on the Analytical Engine?
practice.solution: Ada Lovelace wrote the first published algorithm intended for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, making her the first programmer. Grace Hopper pioneered COBOL and coined 'debugging'.
practice.shortcut: Ada = first program (on paper); Hopper = COBOL + debugging. Don't swap them.

practice.q: The full form of POST, the diagnostic routine that runs when a computer is switched on, is:
practice.solution: POST = Power-On Self-Test: the BIOS/UEFI checks RAM, keyboard, disk controllers etc. before handing over to the boot loader. A failed POST usually beeps.
practice.shortcut: 'Self-Test' is the giveaway - any option without 'Self-Test' is wrong.

practice.q: Which technology was used in the **first** generation of computers?
practice.solution: First-generation machines (ENIAC, UNIVAC-I, EDVAC) were built around **vacuum tubes**, which made them room-sized, hot and unreliable.
practice.shortcut: 1st = tube, 2nd = transistor, 3rd = IC, 4th = chip-CPU.

practice.q: **Jack Kilby** is associated with the invention of the —
practice.solution: **Jack Kilby** built the first **Integrated Circuit** in 1958 at Texas Instruments; Robert Noyce developed the planar version soon after. The transistor (1947) is Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley at Bell Labs.
practice.shortcut: Kilby = Chip. Transistor = Bell Labs trio (1947).

practice.q: **IBM 360**, a family of computers released in 1964, belongs to which generation?
practice.solution: **IBM System/360** used **Integrated Circuits** and supported operating systems — the defining technology of the **third generation** (1964–71).
practice.shortcut: 360 → three → third generation.

practice.q: **EDSAC**, built at Cambridge University in 1949, is remembered as the first —
practice.solution: **EDSAC** (Electronic Delay Storage Automatic Calculator), built under Maurice Wilkes, ran its first program in **1949** and was the first practical **stored-program** computer — instructions and data lived in the same memory.
practice.shortcut: EDSAC = 'S' for Storage → stored program.

practice.q: Which machine is regarded as the first **general-purpose electronic digital** computer?
practice.solution: **ENIAC** (Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer), completed in 1946, was the first electronic computer that could be reprogrammed for any task — hence general-purpose.
practice.shortcut: ENIAC 1946 = first electronic general-purpose.

practice.q: The **Atanasoff–Berry Computer (ABC)** of 1942 is honoured in computer history as the —
options: First computer with a graphical interface
practice.solution: The **ABC**, built by John Atanasoff and Clifford Berry, was the first **electronic digital** computer, though it was special-purpose and never sold. ENIAC (1946) was the first *general-purpose* one.
practice.shortcut: ABC comes before ENIAC alphabetically and historically.

practice.q: The first **microprocessor**, released by Intel in 1971, was the —
practice.solution: The **Intel 4004** (1971) placed a complete CPU on one chip — the first commercial **microprocessor**, which opened the fourth generation.
practice.shortcut: 4004 = four digits, fourth generation.

practice.q: Which feature is the defining characteristic of **fifth-generation** computers?
practice.solution: Fifth-generation work centres on **artificial intelligence**: machines that accept natural language and voice, use parallel processing and ULSI chips, and support robotics. Vacuum tubes, drums and punched cards belong to the first-generation era.
practice.shortcut: 5th gen talks to you — natural language + AI.

practice.q: A key software development that appeared during the **third generation** was the —
practice.solution: With IC-based hardware, third-generation machines ran **operating systems** that managed multiprogramming, and used keyboards and monitors instead of punched cards. Web browsers belong to the 1990s (fourth generation and later).
practice.shortcut: OS + keyboard + monitor = 3rd generation marks.

practice.q: Arrange the technologies in the order computers used them: A. Microprocessor B. Transistor C. Vacuum tube D. Integrated Circuit
practice.solution: Ladder order: vacuum tube (1st) → transistor (2nd) → IC (3rd) → microprocessor (4th), i.e. **C, B, D, A**.
practice.shortcut: V-T-I-M: 'Very Tiny ICs Multiply'.

practice.q: Which generation of computers **directly followed** the integrated-circuit generation?
practice.solution: ICs define the third generation (1964–71); the **fourth generation** (1971 onwards) followed it, built around the **microprocessor**.
practice.shortcut: IC (3rd) → chip-CPU (4th) → AI (5th).

practice.q: Which of the following is the **correct descending** order of computers by size and processing power?
practice.solution: The ladder is **Super → Mainframe → Mini → Micro**: the supercomputer is the fastest and largest, the personal computer the smallest.
practice.shortcut: 'Some Ministers Must Promise' = Super, Main, Mini, PC.

practice.q: A tablet and a laptop are both examples of —
practice.solution: Every single-user personal device — desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone — is a **microcomputer**. 'Micro' refers to the class (CPU on microprocessor chips, one user), not to the physical smallness of a tablet.
practice.shortcut: One user = micro, whatever the shape.

practice.q: A university department provides **many students simultaneous logins** on one mid-sized multi-user machine. This is the classic role of a —
practice.solution: Mid-size, **multi-user departmental** work (tens to hundreds of users) is the textbook role of a **minicomputer** (classic example: PDP-11). Mainframes serve thousands of users; micros serve one.
practice.shortcut: Department with dozens of users = mini.

practice.q: Digital computers represent all data using —
practice.solution: A **digital** computer converts every input into **discrete binary values (0 and 1)** and computes on them. Continuous quantities are the domain of analog machines.
practice.shortcut: Digital = 0/1 digits; analog = smooth needle.

practice.q: A petrol-pump unit that **measures the flow of fuel continuously** and then **computes and prints the price in rupees** works on which principle?
practice.solution: Measuring the continuous fuel flow is the **analog** part; converting it to a digital rupee amount is the **digital** part. A machine combining both is a **hybrid computer**.
practice.shortcut: Petrol pump and ICU monitor = the two hybrid classics.

practice.q: Which statement about **analog computers** is correct?
options: They work on discrete binary digits
They are faster than all digital supercomputers
They were invented in the fourth generation
practice.solution: Analog computers **measure** continuous quantities — temperature, pressure, voltage, speed — and work directly on those signals. They predate digital machines and are not used for general computing today.
practice.shortcut: Analog = 'a needle that slides', not digits.

practice.q: Long-range **weather forecasting and nuclear simulation** are typical applications of —
practice.solution: One gigantic scientific computation at a time is the supercomputer's job — weather models, nuclear simulations, space and defence research.
practice.shortcut: Weather + nuclear = supercomputer.

practice.q: A computer kept at home and used by **one student at a time** is a —
practice.solution: Single-user personal machines — desktops and laptops — are **microcomputers** (personal computers).
practice.shortcut: One user at home = micro.

practice.q: A bank maintains **lakhs of customer accounts** and processes thousands of transactions every minute for many branches at once. The most suitable machine is a —
practice.solution: Very large, simultaneous **bulk transaction processing** for thousands of users is exactly what **mainframes** (e.g. IBM zSeries) are built for.
practice.shortcut: Banks and railways = mainframe; speed for many users, not one big formula.

practice.q: **PARAM 8000**, delivered in 1991, made India one of the few countries able to build supercomputers. It was developed by —
practice.solution: **PARAM 8000** (1991) was built by **C-DAC** (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing), Pune, set up in 1988 after the USA refused to sell India a Cray supercomputer.
practice.shortcut: PARAM = C-DAC, Pune. Not ISRO, not BARC.

practice.q: The full form of **C-DAC**, the centre that built the PARAM series, is —
options: Centre for Development of Advanced Computing
Centre for Defence Analysis and Computing
practice.solution: **C-DAC = Centre for Development of Advanced Computing**, an organisation under the Department of Information Technology, headquartered in Pune.
practice.shortcut: Development, not Digital — the classic trap.

practice.q: Who is known as the **father of the supercomputer**?
practice.solution: **Seymour Cray** (USA) designed the Cray series and is called the **father of the supercomputer**. Dr Vijay Bhatkar is honoured as the father of Indian supercomputing (PARAM).
practice.shortcut: Cray builds Cray — same name.

practice.q: Which unit of the CPU **coordinates and controls** all other units but does not perform calculations?
practice.solution: The **Control Unit (CU)** fetches, decodes and sends direction signals — the traffic constable. All arithmetic and logic belong to the ALU.
practice.shortcut: CU = Constable, Untouched by maths.

practice.q: The **fastest** data-holding locations inside a computer are —
practice.solution: **Registers** are tiny slots **inside the CPU itself** — the fastest storage in the whole machine. Cache comes next, then RAM, then the hard disk.
practice.shortcut: Speed order: Registers > Cache > RAM > Disk.

practice.q: Which register holds the **address of the next instruction** to be executed?
practice.solution: The **Program Counter (PC)** stores the memory address of the *next* instruction. The IR holds the instruction currently being executed; the Accumulator holds ALU results.
practice.shortcut: PC = 'Points to Come'.

practice.q: All **arithmetic and logical** operations of a computer are performed by the —
practice.solution: The **Arithmetic Logic Unit** does the maths (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and the logic (compare, AND, OR).
practice.shortcut: ALU = Actual Labour Unit.

practice.q: The correct sequence of steps in a **machine cycle** is —
practice.solution: The CPU **fetches** the instruction, **decodes** it, **executes** it and **stores** the result — repeating crores of times per second.
practice.shortcut: Fat Dogs Eat Snacks.

practice.q: During **execution** of an instruction, the actual work (say adding two numbers) is done by the —
practice.solution: After fetch and decode, the **execute** step hands real computation to the **ALU**; the CU only supervises, and the PC merely points to the next instruction.
practice.shortcut: Decode is CU's job; the sums are ALU's job.

practice.q: In which machine-cycle step is the **result written back** to memory or a register?
practice.solution: **Store** — the final step saves the executed result into memory or a register before the next fetch begins.
practice.shortcut: Last step = Store.

practice.q: '**Fetching**' an instruction in the machine cycle means —
options: Bringing the instruction from main memory to the CPU
practice.solution: **Fetch** = the CU picks up the next instruction from memory (its address comes from the Program Counter) and places it in the Instruction Register.
practice.shortcut: Fetch = get it, Decode = read it, Execute = do it.

practice.q: Which bus carries the **memory location** (not the data) from the CPU to memory?
practice.solution: The **address bus** carries the location where data is to be read or written. The data itself travels on the data bus, and commands travel on the control bus.
practice.shortcut: Address bus = the house number; data bus = the parcel.

practice.q: In the **von Neumann (stored-program)** architecture, programs and data are —
options: Kept together in the same memory
practice.solution: The stored-program idea places **instructions and data in one memory**, both as numbers, so the CPU can fetch and execute them in sequence — and programs can change without rewiring the machine.
practice.shortcut: One memory for both = von Neumann.

practice.q: The basic working cycle of a computer, **IPO**, stands for —
practice.solution: **Input → Process → Output**: data enters, the CPU works on it, results leave (with Storage keeping them for later).
practice.shortcut: IPO — like a share issue: data in, work done, result out.

practice.q: Which of the following correctly lists the **four basic functions** of a computer?
practice.solution: A computer takes **input**, **processes** it in the CPU, gives **output**, and **stores** data — everything else (gaming, browsing) is an application of these four.
practice.shortcut: IPOS: Input, Process, Output, Storage.

practice.q: Who is known as the **father of the computer** for designing the Analytical Engine?
practice.solution: **Charles Babbage** designed the Difference Engine (1822) and the **Analytical Engine** (1837), the blueprint of the modern computer — hence the father of the computer.
practice.shortcut: Babbage Built the idea.

practice.q: The **Pascaline**, an early mechanical adding machine built in 1642, was invented by —
practice.solution: **Blaise Pascal** built the Pascaline to help his tax-clerk father add long columns of figures. Leibniz later improved on it with a machine that could also multiply.
practice.shortcut: Pascaline → Pascal. The computer language Pascal also honours him.

practice.q: Who is called the **father of theoretical computer science**, known for the 1936 'Turing machine' and the 1950 Turing test?
practice.solution: **Alan Turing** described the Turing machine (a model of computation) in 1936 and proposed the Turing test for machine intelligence in 1950.
practice.shortcut: Turing = Theory + Test.

practice.q: Which translator converts **assembly language mnemonics** (ADD, MOV) into machine code?
practice.solution: An **assembler** translates assembly language (2GL) into machine code. Compilers and interpreters work on high-level languages (3GL).
practice.shortcut: Assembly → Assembler (both start with A).

practice.q: A translator that processes a high-level program **line by line, stopping at the first error**, is a(n) —
practice.solution: An **interpreter** translates and executes one line at a time and stops at the first error — handy for testing. A compiler translates the whole program first.
practice.shortcut: Interpreter = instant, line-by-line.

practice.q: Which statement about a **compiler** is correct?
options: It translates and runs one line at a time
It translates the entire program before execution and reports all errors together
It is not needed for high-level languages
practice.solution: A **compiler** takes the complete source program, produces machine code in one go, and lists **all errors together** — compiled programs then run fast.
practice.shortcut: Compiler = Complete + all errors at once.

practice.q: Before a program written in **C** can run on a computer, it must first be converted into —
options: Machine language by a compiler or interpreter
practice.solution: The CPU executes only **machine language (1GL)**. Every high-level language program (C, Java, Python) must be translated into machine code by a compiler or an interpreter.
practice.shortcut: CPU's mother tongue = 0s and 1s only.

practice.q: Machine language is called the **first generation (1GL)** of programming languages because it —
options: Consists of 0s and 1s that the CPU executes directly, with no translation
Was the first to use a compiler
Runs the fastest on all machines
practice.solution: **1GL = machine language**: pure binary that the processor understands natively. Assembly (2GL) needs an assembler; high-level languages (3GL) need a compiler or interpreter.
practice.shortcut: 1GL needs no translator at all.

practice.q: **SQL**, used to query databases, is generally classified as a —
practice.solution: **SQL is a 4GL** — very high level, close to plain English ('SELECT … FROM …'). 1GL = machine code, 2GL = assembly, HTML is markup, not a language generation.
practice.shortcut: SQL speaks almost English → high generation (4GL).

practice.q: **COBOL** is a high-level language designed mainly for —
practice.solution: **COBOL** (COmmon **Business** Oriented Language, 1959) handles bulk business records — banking and insurance still run on it.
practice.shortcut: COBOL = Common Business.

practice.q: The language chosen for **platform-independent** application development — 'write once, run anywhere' — is —
practice.solution: **Java** (James Gosling) compiles to bytecode that runs on any machine with a Java virtual machine — hence 'write once, run anywhere'.
practice.shortcut: Java = Jugaad-free portability.

practice.q: The full form of **ALU** is —
practice.solution: **ALU = Arithmetic Logic Unit** — the CPU part that does arithmetic and logical operations.
practice.shortcut: ALU: Arithmetic first, Logic second.

practice.q: The full form of **BIOS** is —
practice.solution: **BIOS = Basic Input Output System** — firmware on the motherboard that wakes the hardware and hands over to the operating system.
practice.shortcut: BIOS says hello to the hardware first.

practice.q: **USB**, the standard connector for pen drives and keyboards, stands for —
practice.solution: **USB = Universal Serial Bus** — sends data as a serial stream, connects almost everything (hence universal), and is hot-swappable.
practice.shortcut: Serial = one-by-one bits; Universal = fits everything.

practice.q: The correct expansion of **EPROM** is —
practice.solution: **EPROM = Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory** — it can be erased by **ultraviolet light** and reprogrammed. The 'Electrically' version is EEPROM.
practice.shortcut: EP = Erasable Programmable; EEP = Electrically Erasable Programmable.

practice.q: Which expansion of **EEPROM** is correct?
options: Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory
Extra Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory
Electrically Erasable Programmable Random Access Memory
practice.solution: **EEPROM = Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory** — erased by applying an electrical signal, no UV lamp needed. It is still ROM, not RAM.
practice.shortcut: E-E = Electrically Erasable; the last word stays ROM.

practice.q: **VDU**, another name for the computer monitor, stands for —
practice.solution: **VDU = Visual Display Unit** — the screen on which the computer shows output. 'Video' is the planted wrong word.
practice.shortcut: V = Visual, not Video.

practice.q: **DPI** printed on a printer's specification box measures —
practice.solution: **DPI = Dots Per Inch**, the number of ink dots a printer places in one inch — higher DPI, sharper print. Screens use PPI (pixels per inch).
practice.shortcut: Printers spray dots (DPI); screens light pixels (PPI).

practice.q: **OMR**, used to evaluate answer sheets filled with pencil bubbles, stands for —
practice.solution: **OMR = Optical Mark Recognition** — the machine detects where marks (bubbles) are placed. OCR reads characters; MICR reads magnetic ink.
practice.shortcut: OMR = Marks, OCR = Characters, MICR = Ink.

practice.q: The full form of **LCD**, the technology of most laptop screens, is —
practice.solution: **LCD = Liquid Crystal Display** — crystals twist to block or pass light. LED screens are LCD panels lit by light-emitting diodes.
practice.shortcut: LCD = Liquid Crystal; LED = Light Emitting Diode.

practice.q: Which pair is **wrongly matched**?
practice.solution: The accepted form is **Uninterruptible** Power Supply. The other three pairs are standard expansions.
practice.shortcut: One adjective decides it: Uninterruptible.

practice.q: Which of the following is **NOT** an input or output device term?
practice.solution: **RTOS = Real-Time Operating System**, an OS type. VDU is an output device (monitor); OMR and MICR are input readers.
practice.shortcut: Operating-system words are never device words.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. First-generation computers used magnetic drums for memory.
2. Multiprogramming became practical with the second generation.
3. Integrated circuits made operating systems practical.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 1 is correct — magnetic drums were first-generation memory. Statement 2 is wrong: **multiprogramming belongs to the third generation** (IC era, with OS support). Statement 3 is correct — IC-based third-generation machines ran operating systems.
practice.shortcut: 2nd generation = transistors + languages; OS + multiprogramming = 3rd generation.

practice.q:
Match the machine to its generation:
A. UNIVAC-I  B. IBM 1401  C. IBM 360  D. Intel 4004
practice.solution: UNIVAC-I (1951, vacuum tubes) → 1st; IBM 1401 (transistors) → 2nd; IBM 360 (1964, ICs) → 3rd; Intel 4004 (1971, single-chip CPU) → 4th.
practice.shortcut: The four machines walk the four rungs in order.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. An analog computer works directly on measurements of continuous quantities.
2. Every digital computer is also a hybrid computer.
3. A minicomputer is more powerful than a mainframe.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 1 is the definition of analog computing. Statement 2 is wrong — digital and hybrid are separate classes. Statement 3 is wrong — the mainframe is **more** powerful than a minicomputer (Super → Mainframe → Mini → Micro).
practice.shortcut: Two wrong statements use reversed ladders — check each against its definition.

practice.q: Four computers are arranged as: P (weather simulation), Q (bank's central ledger for thousands of branches), R (a college department server for 60 users), S (a student's laptop). Which assignment of class is correct?
practice.solution: One giant scientific problem → **supercomputer**; thousands of simultaneous transactions → **mainframe**; department-level multi-user → **minicomputer**; single personal user → **microcomputer**.
practice.shortcut: Workload size maps to the ladder rung: one problem / one organisation / one department / one person.

practice.q:
Match the CPU register to its job:
A. Program Counter  B. Instruction Register  C. Accumulator  D. Memory Address Register
options: A-current instruction, B-next instruction's address, C-ALU result, D-address being accessed in memory
A-ALU result, B-current instruction, C-next instruction's address, D-address being accessed in memory
A-next instruction's address, B-current instruction, C-ALU result, D-address being accessed in memory
A-next instruction's address, B-ALU result, C-current instruction, D-address being accessed in memory
practice.solution: **PC** points to the next instruction; **IR** holds the instruction being executed; the **Accumulator** collects ALU results; the **MAR** holds the memory address currently being read or written.
practice.shortcut: PC-Next, IR-Now, ACC-Answer, MAR-Address.

practice.q:
Consider the statements about the system bus:
1. The data bus carries information in both directions.
2. The address bus is unidirectional, from CPU to memory.
3. The width of the data bus decides how many bits move at a time.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are standard: data flows both ways on the **data bus**; the **address bus** goes one way (CPU → memory); a '32-bit/64-bit' label on a processor describes the **data-bus/register width**.
practice.shortcut: Data both ways, address one way, width = bits at once.

practice.q:
Match the person to the contribution:
A. Herman Hollerith  B. Grace Hopper  C. Douglas Engelbart  D. Tim Berners-Lee
options: A-computer mouse, B-COBOL and early compiler, C-punched-card tabulating machine, D-World Wide Web
A-punched-card tabulating machine, B-World Wide Web, C-computer mouse, D-COBOL and early compiler
A-punched-card tabulating machine, B-COBOL and early compiler, C-computer mouse, D-World Wide Web
A-COBOL and early compiler, B-punched-card tabulating machine, C-World Wide Web, D-computer mouse
practice.solution: Hollerith's punched-card machine processed the 1890 US Census (his firm fed into IBM); Hopper pioneered COBOL and wrote an early **compiler**; Engelbart built the first **mouse**; Berners-Lee created the **WWW**.
practice.shortcut: Census, COBOL, click, web — four different decades, four different people.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Assembly language needs an assembler, not a compiler.
2. A 4GL such as SQL is closer to human language than C.
3. HTML is a third-generation programming language.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are standard (assembly → assembler; SQL is a 4GL near plain English). Statement 3 is wrong: **HTML is a markup language**, not a programming language at any GL level.
practice.shortcut: The HTML option is almost always the planted error.

practice.q:
Match the technology to its typical use:
A. OMR  B. OCR  C. MICR  D. DPI
options: A-bank cheque code line, B-pencil-marked answer sheets, C-print resolution, D-scanning printed text into editable form
A-pencil-marked answer sheets, B-bank cheque code line, C-scanning printed text into editable form, D-print resolution
A-pencil-marked answer sheets, B-scanning printed text into editable form, C-bank cheque code line, D-print resolution
A-print resolution, B-scanning printed text into editable form, C-pencil-marked answer sheets, D-bank cheque code line
practice.solution: **OMR** detects marks (bubbles), **OCR** reads characters into editable text, **MICR** reads the magnetic-ink code line on cheques, and **DPI** (dots per inch) measures print resolution.
practice.shortcut: Marks, Characters, Ink, Dots — one word per technology.

practice.q: Which set of expansions is **fully correct**?
options: UPS – Uninterruptible Power Supply; POST – Power-On Self-Test; VDU – Visual Display Unit
UPS – Uninterrupted Power Supply; POST – Power On System Test; VDU – Video Display Unit
UPS – Uninterruptible Power Supply; POST – Power On System Test; VDU – Visual Display Unit
UPS – Uninterrupted Power Supply; POST – Power-On Self-Test; VDU – Video Display Unit
practice.solution: The three fixed traps in one row: **Uninterruptible**, **Power-On Self-Test**, **Visual** Display Unit. Every other set contains at least one wrong word.
practice.shortcut: Memorise the trap row once — it answers all variants.
